messages.subject_clean: Huge standard errors with N-mixture – can I share information across sites?
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am new to ‘unmarked’ and would really appreciate some help with a couple of questions. The first relates to some extremely large estimates of standard errors, and the second is about how I should interpret the abundance estimates from pcount/N-mixture.

Study design: I have a nested design with 28 independent study sites, each containing a transect of 14 cameras. Cameras within a study site are not truly independent i.e. there is a small chance the same individual could be detected at a neighbouring camera.

Aim: My aim is to derive and compare estimates of wallaby abundance at each of the 28 study sites. Given the nested design, with cameras not truly independent, I am happy for the interpretation to be something like "estimated wallaby abundance at an average camera within a study site", or even to just be a detectability-corrected index of wallaby abundance.

I have played around with a simple pcount() / N-mixture model (5 temporal replicates at each camera). The model is: Detection ~ lure age + Julian date, Abundance ~ study site

Now, if I predict from this model to each of the 28 independent study sites, I get 28 estimates of abundance with SE/CI’s. The problem is that a small number of study sites had no wallaby detections at any of the 14 cameras. At those study sites, the model estimates that abundance is essentially zero with extremely large or infinite se’s/CI’s. I imagine this is because there isn’t any information from those sites.

Biologically speaking though, I am very confident that the abundance of wallabies is very low at these sites and would intuitively expect a confidence interval that reflects this.

I have two main questions:

1. Is there a better way of going about the analysis so that I could estimate a more realistic confidence interval at the sites with no wallaby detections? Perhaps a way that shares information in a better way from the broader dataset (i.e. the sites with wallaby detections)?

2. The nested design is messing with my head a bit in terms of interpretation. Do you think predicting a single estimate for each of the 28 independent study sites could be interpreted as the estimated abundance of wallabies on an average camera at each study site?

Any thoughts are greatly appreciated!! Thank you!

Hi Calum,

One thing that comes to mind is that you are  estimating 31 parameters and 28 of these are abundance-related, so even with 392 sites, a desirable level of precision may be too much to ask. Using a less parameterized model--maybe using covariates to try to tease apart differences in abundance rather than estimating a different  intercept for each site--might help. Or you might treat the effect of site as a random effect: couldn't use unmarked, but could use whatever Bayesian tool you prefer..

One other thing to look at is whether some of these sites with few or no detections also happen to have lure ages or Julian dates associated with much lower detection probabilities. If sites xyz have no detections but were also sampled during a time of year where estimated detection is more difficult, then tough to tease apart N/p.

John

Hi Ohad,

I am not the most experienced unmarked user, but I think I could give you some advice, as I was in your position not long ago (MSc thesis). Your question is too broad to be answered with the information you provide, you need to ask more precisely what you don't understand from the model output. You may not understand a single thing, which is perfectly fine, we all started knowing nothing. If that is the case, I recommend you to first search information about generalized linear models, and specifically logistic models. There are plenty of articles about it. Also, there are good explanations on the outputs of these models in youtube, for example.

It would help to help you if you mention what are your objectives, what you want to assess/test, and what are the meaning of your covariates. From your model, I wonder what "proximity.x" represents, and if this covariate is meaningful for explaining the variation in the data for the ecological process (occupancy in this case). I also wonder if you are using covariates for the detection probability in any of your models. If you have doubts about the meaning of detection and/or occupancy parameters, I would recommend you to read the article of Guillera-Arroita (2017) published in Ecography, it summarises the advances in occupancy models and provides excellent figures to understand both observation and ecological process.

I hope this helps, maybe more experienced users can give their own advice.

Regards,

José.

messages.body_plain:
Ohad,

I like and agree with José's response. Like José, I'm no expert on occupancy modeling, and I'm currently finishing my MS thesis using occupancy modeling on songbirds. For my research, I took a 5 day "Presence" workshop before I felt confident running these models and interpreting results, so keep an eye out for workshops on the unmarked and presence websites. Even if you plan on doing everything in unmarked, the presence workshop is invaluable for understanding the process and getting started. Some good resources for understanding and practicing logistic regression and GLMs in R can be found at https://highstat.com/index.php/mixed-effects-models-and-extensions-in-ecology-with-r. There are other books/manuals there as well, but for me this book and practice data sets were free from my university library, so you might want to check with your library for this or similar books. With all that said, I will take a shot at addressing your question.

The detection part of your formula: occu(formula = ~1 ~ ...., data = umf),is the null model/intercept only model of detection; this is basically saying that detection is constant and that your not modeling the influence of any sampling covariate (temperature, moon phase) on the detection probability. For interpreting this value, R might have a function called "inv.logit". If you take the parameter estimate of detection (the intercept) and apply the inverse logit function to that number, that is the estimate of detection probability.
However, I, and from what I know many others, typically define a set of a priori hypothetical models of detection like:
 Det.Null <- occu(formula = ~1 ~ 1, data = umf)
 Det.Mod.1 <- occu(formula = ~ Temp ~ 1, data = umf)
 Det.Mod .2 <- occu(formula = ~ Moon ~ 1, data = umf)
 Det.Mod .3 <- occu(formula = ~ Temp + Moon ~ 1, data = umf)

This set of models would then be ranked with AIC, and the variable(s) in the top tanked model would be carried on to subsequent occupancy models, so if "Temp" was the covariate that best explained detection, the occupancy models built/assessed afterwards would include this like:
Occ.Mod <- occu(formula = ~ Temp ~ proximity.xnear, data = umf)

The a priori approach is not a rule, and some may disagree with my framing, but the same approach could be taken with the occupancy portion of the modeling procedure.

With your call summary posted with in you question, the same goes for using the inverse logit function on the intercept to get occupancy probability. One note is that this back transformation is only relevant to your state-based parameter estimates (Detection intercept & Occupancy intercept); this transformation takes the estimate from the logit scale to the probability scale. Additionally, since you've used a categorical variable with 2 levels, the intercept of the occupancy portion is also the reference. Although not reported in the output,"far" is the reference category at the intercept, and "near" is being compared to that reference. What you have reported indicates that the "near" category positively influences occupancy probability when compared the the "far" category. The default in R is to set the reference alphabetically, but you could re-level your categories to switch that comparison (and make other comparisons).

Lastly, and I may be wrong on this interpretation, the intercept is the parameter estimate when all the covariates equal 0. I believe you could think of this as the average detection/occupancy probability. Also this value will be the point where the predicted occupancy curve/line would cross the y-axis of any graphical predictions you make.

If you need more clarification, or even samples of code for this process, model selection, model evaluation, and making predictions, you should feel free to email me directly - I know exactly what is feels like to be in your shoes.

Good luck!

Dan Hannon

Thanks a lot for your response, John – much appreciated!

I get what you're saying about having many abundance-related parameters, and that using covariates would reduce the number of parameters. Unfortunately, we only have covariates at the level of the independent study site, and they only explain a moderate amount of variation.

The reason I am after an estimate of abundance for each of the 28 study sites is because this estimate will be fed into a structural equation model involving many other species. The other species are represented by unique estimates of abundance at each study site, which I’ve mostly estimated using CMR.

I think your second suggestion is unlikely in our dataset - Julian date and lure age only have small effects, and the sites with zero detections were basically randomly distributed across the year, so I don’t think there is any confounding of the detection process and N as a result.

I think the reason for the large or infinite standard errors is that we are estimating an abundance intercept for each study site, and some of the study sites had no wallaby detections. I still intuitively feel like for sites with no detections, we should be fairly confident of a low population size, based on many detections of the species at other sites.

So, if you think a Bayesian approach using a site-level random effect is the only way to estimate the uncertainty around the estimates of abundance for sites with zero detections, are you able to point me in the direction of any papers/code/suggestions that could get me started on this?

In other words, I would like to see if jackals tend to use more sites where the abundance of large carnivores is greater/lower for example (I just used a standardized measure of relative abundance as a proxy for the intensity of use -i.e capture rates, to help us develop further hypothesis…).

Since I am more interested in the effect of each of the covariates rather than a particular model, I decided to run a model average (also because each individual model developed very low w), and now I want to calculate the importance of each automatically, however, I am receiving some errors (script below). But as a starting point, these aren't results yet--more like an update on where the model is currently sampling and how the algorithm has performed so far.

John

I am using count data as my dependent variable, and individual transects are my sampling unit, however my transects have variable effective sampling areas.

I have two very distinct vegetation types for the data, open and closed, which significantly impacts the detection of wildlife.
Prior to using 'unmarked' I determined the effective strip width (ESW) of each vegetation class, and then by controlling for the proportion of each vegetation class along each transect, I determined the effective sample area of each transect.
How do I take this into account in 'unmarked' thought? Should I create an offset term of my effective sampling area?

Perhaps I am thinking about this wrong though and because the model is hierarchical it is taking detection into account already, and thus is it not good to determine ESW beforehand?
If so, then how/where can this be included?
What I have is wildlife count per transect, but each transect has a count of wildlife in open vegetation and a count of wildlife in closed vegetation, and the length of each transect in each vegetation class is different along each transect. Hence my problem!

distsamp requires a transect level format, which is why I thought creating an offset term for each transect would be good. But if not, I have read that the function ForestDistData can be used to convert my individual-level distance data to the transect-level format. In the meantime, Anna, you can remove unused factor levels using code like this:

siteCovs(umf.sub) <- droplevels(siteCovs(umf.sub))

In terms of software for analysis, you basically have 3 options:
1) package unmarked in R
2) program Distance
3) write a custom model in your software of choice
Of those 3, if you have the statistical and programming chops to write your own model, then go for it! A custom model is the only way to add an autocorrelation term or the type of random effect you want. Autocorrelation is typically incorporated as a variance-covariance matrix on the errors/residuals of a linear model. There is a random effect in unmarked models, but it refers to the unobserved, "true" abundance at each sampling location (as opposed to the mean abundance across locations, which is the abundance estimate that the model returns in the results). A third advantage of a custom model would be to propagate uncertainty around chimp nest decay rates through the model. However, it takes a lot of knowledge and/or effort to write your own model, so if you're not going that route, I'd recommend unmarked. It fits a lot of different models and allows for easier incorporation of covariates of abundance than does program Distance.

If you're fitting a model in unmarked, you could include site as a fixed effect. There's nothing wrong with that approach. In terms of autocorrelation, are you concerned about autocorrelation in that chimps don't nest independently, and individuals in a group will all nest near one another? People often deal with that type of autocorrelation by modeling the number of clusters/groups of individuals rather than the number of individuals (if you can easily define clusters). Or are you concerned about autocorrelation that could arise if/when chimps preferentially go back to the same area to nest, resulting in spatial correlation that forms over time? That's tricky. Do you know how other nest-based surveys deal with that issue? I guess I'd start by fitting a model in unmarked and testing for autocorrelation in the residuals. I'm curious what other folks will have to say.

Philip Shirk

messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I have been using gdistsamp to analyse survey data for a nocturnal, burrow-nesting species. I have found that models using data truncated to different distances give very different predictions of total population size. The more the data are truncated, the larger the population prediction. The structure of the top model is consistent across differently truncated data sets and GOF is good in each case. We are wondering whether the study system is just not suited to this type of model.

The species is not visible by day but vocalisations can be elicited by playing a recording of its call. We used point distance sampling, where an observer played the call at the central point and recorded the number of responses in each distance band. Not all individuals will respond on every occasion, and we have treated response rate as the availability part of the model. If an individual responds it is 'available' for detection. However, both response rate and detection probability are expected to decline with increasing distance from the observer.

I am struggling to get my head around whether the detection function part of the model will 'mop up' this possible decline in availability over distance. If not, is there another method I can use to account for this variation? Could this be the cause of the varying population estimates I get when including different distance bands?

Any advice would be much appreciated. I am happy to provide more information if needed.

Thanks,

Zoe

messages.body_plain:
Confounding availability with distance is a problem. First, it pretty much ensures that the average availability varies across sites. Some sites will happen to more burrows close to the survey point, and therefore will have a higher average (over the whole site) availability, while other sites will happen to have more burrows further away from the survey point, and therefore will have lower average availability. The variation in availability across sites is a problem because the model that unmarked fits with gdistsamp uses data from all the sites to estimate availability in the same way that point count estimates use data from all the sites to estimate a constant detection probability. We know that violation of the assumption of constant detection probability in the point-count models can bias estimates pretty badly, so violation of the assumption of constant availability in the gdistsamp model is a pretty big concern. Second, even if the model were able to accurately estimate availability from the replicate surveys, the estimate of detectability will be biased low (and hence the abundance estimate biased high) because of the overlap between availability and detectability with regards to distance.

However, if it's sensible to assume that "availability" is very nearly 1 at a distance of 0 (i.e. the animal will vocalize if you play the recording at the entrance to its burrow and the observer will hear it), then you can simply analyze the data in a standard distance sampling context with the "detectability" defined as the composite probability that an individual vocalizes and the observer hears it. You'd still want to watch out for large differences among predicted abundances if you truncate the data a bit or use different detection functions.

If still possible, it may be better to conduct the surveys a little differently.
Option 1 (a little more field work, & more modeling effort): try to estimate availability independently. You could do this by setting up speakers at varying distances from burrows, playing calls, and observing (from right next to the borrow) whether or not the animal responds. In this scenario, "availability" is defined as the animal vocalizing, and "detectability" is defined as your ability to hear the vocalization. Once you have an estimate of availability, you could fit a model where the probability of observing any given individual in each distance bin is the combination of availability (a known value at that distance) * detectability (an estimated value at that distance).
Option 2: if it's sensible to assume that a given occupied burrow is always occupied by the same individual, I think it would be worthwhile identifying the individual burrow that each call comes from and then analyzing in a mark-recapture framework.
Option 3: use transect-based distance-sampling surveys to look for the burrows themselves and model burrow densities. Then get an independent estimate of burrow occupancy and adjust estimates of burrow density accordingly.

Philip Shirk

Hi Zoe,

-Does the sampling consist of one visit to each point with multiple time intervals, or multiple visits to each point? If the former, I have a little trouble wrapping my head around the meaning of the dynamics--I guess M_i is the population around the point during the visit and N_i,t is the subset that calls within a given interval? I guess this makes sense if you count each individual during each interval in which it calls.

--If the data are structured such that your count by band only includes individuals in the first occasion in which they call, I think you would get positive bias, and it might make sense to sum these counts and use distsamp.

--Re. distance-related heterogeneity in availability, I think the model should be robust to this. I believe one of the simulation studies in Chandler et al. 2011 deals with this (in the context of movement rather than call rate, but same idea, I think). I think if phi is some half-normal function and p is some half normal function, you can still estimate of N/M by treating phi as a constant and p as a half-normal, but the sigma estimate for p will be much smaller than p's 'true' sigma. In other words, the product of two HN's can look a lot like the product of a binomial constant and an HN with a distinct smaller sigma. A quick sanity check (script at bottom) suggests so. The CI coverage may be permissive, however.

-Re. phi~response rate: I don't think I would use a covariate derived from the observations to model variation in the observations.

John

sigma2<-7 ##decay for putative p

p2<-exp(-z^2/(2*sigma2^2)) ##HN decay for p
y<-rbinom(1500, 50, p1*p2) ##data--say we know each distance band at each site has 50 animals

  i.phi<-starts[1]
  lsig<-starts[2]

  sigma<-exp(lsig)
  p2est<-exp(-z^2/(2*sigma^2))
  ll<-sum(dbinom(y, 50, p2est*phi, log=TRUE))

}

###fit it

###Note estimates are 'wrong'

phiest<-inv.logit(fit$estimate[1])
p2est<-exp(-z^2/(2*exp(fit$estimate[2])^2))

###plot the true function underlying the observations

Dear Asif,

I allow myself to make some comments here: I don't think that statistical analysis should work like this. When you use such techniques, you ought to have a minimum of basic knowledge yourself, or else you should not use these methods. Therefore, I strongly suggest you spend a week or two, or more, if you need, to get a basic understanding of regression models (Nmix models are a sort of hierarchical regression models) so that you do understand the fundamentals yourself. Otherwise, the risk of misuse of statistical techniques is too great.

The web is full with resources that you can use for learning the basics that you need. Or you can surely get pirate versions of introductory books, such as my own book from 2010 in Academic Press or Korner et al. (~2017) or COUNTLESS others. (Of course you can also purchase such books.)

As always, on lists such as this one, one should always do one's homework first, before asking. Just coming with nothing at all and ask the group "Please do my work for me", that's not how it should be done.

Sorry for being so honest here.

Best regards -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vaughn,

yearlySiteCovs in unmarkedframeGDS objects are the equivalent of obsCovs in other single-season objects like unmarkedFrame objects. Richard notes this in the gdistsamp documentation, but the "years" in these objects are visits/surveys; with the term "year" being a hold-over from the colext (multiseason occupancy) model that preceded gdistsamp. The smallest observation units in unmarkedframeGDS are the counts within distance bins within a single visit to a site; instead of being predicted by obsCovs (as in models like occu, pcount, etc.), these data are fit with a detection function (halfnorm, hazard, exp, or uniform). It looks like what you list as observation level covariates (behaviour, age class, and detection mode) are individual-specific (within-bin?) characteristics that aren't accommodated by gdistSamp ... though there's probably some way to do this in a Bayesian/BUGS/JAGS framework.

HTH

Giancarlo
